title: Testing an API end to end

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 1.1 — TypeScript for API testing

Six concepts, six runnable cells. Everything tomorrow's API tests are built from.

> **Every Run starts fresh.** The studio executes your code in a new process each time, so nothing is left over between runs.
>
> **`Identifier 'x' has already been declared`?** Cells share one workspace, so re-running

| # | Concept | Why an API test needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `let` vs `const` | The token is made in one place, used in another. |
| 2 | Template literals | Glue a runtime token into a header. |
| 3 | Objects | A request body *is* an object. |
| 4 | Nested access | The answer is a tree you walk. |
| 5 | `async` / `await` | Every call answers later, not now. |
| 6 | Destructuring | How a test asks for its tools. |

## 1. `let` vs `const`

`const` = this name always points here. `let` = can be repointed later.

Your token doesn't exist when the file starts — it arrives after a login call. So it needs
a name that exists early and gets filled in later. That's `let`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. Template literals

A string in backticks (`` ` ``), where `${...}` drops a value into the text. The backtick
key sits left of `1`.

```ts
`token=${token}`
```

const authToken = "abc123";

console.log("with plus:      " + "token=" + authToken);   // easy to lose a space
console.log(`with backticks: token=${authToken}`);        // readable

const nightlyPrice = 111;
console.log(`Total is ${nightlyPrice * 2} for two nights`);   // any expression works

console.log(`spans
two lines`);                                              // quotes can't do this

**Expected:** the first two lines both print `token=abc123` — that's the point.

**Where it shows up:** every authenticated call tomorrow carries
`` headers: { Cookie: `token=${token}` } ``. The token differs every run, so it *must* be
built at runtime.

**Challenge:** set `id = 3652` and print `booking/3652`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 3. Objects

Named values in curly braces. A value can be another object — that's how you get a second
level. Objects are the language of APIs: you send one, you get one back.

**Expected:** `admin`, `2018-01-01`, then the booking printed across several lines.

Watch the quotes: `111` is a number, `"111"` is a string, and some APIs reject the wrong one.

**Challenge:** add a `contact` object with an `email`, then print just the email.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 4. Reading a nested value

Walk down with dots, one per level. Take a wrong turn and you don't get an error *there* —
you get `undefined`, and the error appears on the **next** dot. That's what makes this
confusing the first time.

**Expected:** `3652`, `Jim`, `2018-01-01`

**`Cannot read properties of undefined` means an *earlier* dot was wrong.** The cure is
always the same and takes five seconds:

```ts
console.log(JSON.stringify(response, null, 2));
```

Look at the real shape, then write the path. Guessing twice is slower than looking once.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 5. `async` / `await`

A network call can't answer instantly, so you get a **Promise** — an IOU. `await` means
"wait here until it's paid, then give me the real value."

Every API call is async. Miss one `await` and you're checking the status of an IOU.

**Expected:**

```
without await: Promise { <pending> }
with await:    abc123
```

That first line is the whole lesson. See `Promise { <pending> }` anywhere and you've missed
an `await`.

**Two awaits per API call:** `await api.post(...)` for the response, then `await res.json()`
to read it. Forgetting the second is the common slip.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 6. Destructuring

Pull named values out of an object in one line. It's how Playwright hands you your tools:
`async ({ request }) => {}` means "of everything you offer, I want `request`".

**Expected:** `3652 Jim Brown 3652`

That rename form appears tomorrow as
`const { bookingid: id, booking } = await created.json();` — two values, one shortened, one line.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `let` vs `const` | Filled in later → `let`, declared outside. |
| Template literals | `` `token=${token}` `` for runtime values. |
| Objects | Numbers and booleans go unquoted. |
| Nested access | `undefined` blames an *earlier* dot — print the object. |
| `async` / `await` | Two per call: response, then `.json()`. |
| Destructuring | `{ request }` is a test asking for tools. |

**Next:** [Day 1.2 — Testing an API end to end](/learn/w8/d1/p2)

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 1.2 — Testing an API end to end

You'll log into a real API, create a booking, read it back, get refused without a token,
update it two ways, delete it, and prove it's gone. **No browser. About five seconds.**
The same journey clicked through a UI takes closer to thirty.

Prerequisites: [Day 1.1](/learn/w8/d1/p1).

> **Mode: explore.** Write code in the editor and press Run — it drives a real browser and shows you what happened.

## Why test the API, not just the UI

A click sends a message to a server. Testing that message directly buys you three things:

| | Through the UI | Through the API |
|---|---|---|
| Create-and-verify | ~25–30 s | ~3 s |
| Can start | once screens exist | as soon as the endpoint does — often weeks earlier |
| Fails when | a button moves, a class is renamed | behaviour actually changed |

That last row is the one people underestimate: UI tests fail for cosmetic reasons, API tests
mostly fail when something is really wrong. Hence the pyramid — many API tests, fewer UI ones.

## The app, and reading its docs

**Restful Booker** — `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com`
([docs](https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html)). A small public bookings API.

> **Why not the banking app?** It has no documented public API, and API testing needs one.
> Week 8 is the exception, and uses this one throughout.

Reading the docs *is* the first skill. Before any code, you need five facts:

| What | For the login call |
|---|---|
| Host | `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com` |
| Endpoint | `/auth` |
| Method | `POST` |
| Send | `{ "username": "admin", "password": "password123" }` |
| Expect | `200` + `{ "token": "..." }` |

### Where API docs come from

Developers publish docs with a tool. Two names cover most of what you'll meet:

| Tool | What it also does |
|---|---|
| **Swagger / OpenAPI** | generated from the API's own definition, so it can't drift out of date |
| **Postman** | manual API testing *and* publishing docs from the same saved collection |

Postman is worth knowing for both halves — you'll poke an endpoint by hand before automating
it, and your team may publish its documentation from there.

Doc quality varies enormously, and it decides how long your job takes. A page stating the
response shape per endpoint saves you guessing. One that doesn't means you probe the API
yourself — which is what the next few cells do, and a habit worth keeping either way.

## Head and body, authentication and authorization

Every request splits in two: the **header** carries instructions *about* the message, the
**body** carries the data. (Body is also called *data* or *payload* — same thing.)

| Header | Says |
|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | "my data is in this format" |
| `Authorization` / `Cookie` | "here's proof of who I am" |

**Authentication** = who are you (username + password). **Authorization** = what may you do
(the token you got back). You authenticate once, then attach the token to everything after.

A token is a short-lived proof it's you — same idea as an OTP. It expires, which is exactly
why your test must fetch a fresh one at runtime instead of pasting yesterday's into the file.

## Example 1 — get a token

**Objective:** POST credentials to `/auth`, get a token.

| Line | Does |
|---|---|
| `request.newContext()` | Opens a reusable API connection. No browser starts. |
| `api.post(url, { data })` | Sends POST; Playwright turns `data` into JSON. |
| `res.status()` | Status code, as a number. |
| `res.json()` | Parses the body into an object you can use dots on. |

**Expected:** `status: 200` and a token like `25b3f24d16a6fbe`. Yours will differ — that's
what makes it a token.

**Challenge:** use a wrong password and re-run. The status is still **200** — the failure is
described *in the body*. That's why checking only the status code isn't enough.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 2 — create a booking

**Objective:** send a booking, capture the id the server invents.

**Expected:** `200`, then `{ "bookingid": 3652, "booking": { ... } }`

Three things worth stopping on:

| Observation | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Returned **`200`, not `201`** | `201 Created` is the *convention*, not a rule. Assert what your API does. |
| **No token sent, and it worked** | Creating is open here. Don't assume every call needs auth. |
| The **id came from the server** | You couldn't know it in advance. |

That third one is the most important habit in API testing: **create your own data, read back
its id, use that.** Never hardcode an id you found by hand — it'll be gone tomorrow.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 3 — read it back

**Objective:** fetch by id, and meet a shape change.

**Expected:** `200`, and the booking — but look at the shape.

- **Create** wrapped it: `createdBody.booking.firstname`
- **Read** doesn't: `fetchedBody.firstname`

Same data, two shapes, one API. Assume they match and you get `Cannot read properties of
undefined` — the Day 1.1 error. Same fix: print the body, then write the path.

The URL uses backticks because the id is only known at runtime.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 4 — the token earns its keep

**Objective:** update without a token, then with one. Creating was open; changing is not.

**Expected:**

```
no token   -> 403 Forbidden
with token -> 200
firstname:  James
```

**403 is what a missing or wrong token looks like.** See 403 — or a message like "bad
credential" — and suspect the token first, not your data.

### Bearer or Cookie?

This API wants `` Cookie: `token=${token}` ``. Many others want
`` Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` ``. Both mean "proof of identity, in a header". Which one
is not guessable — the docs say, and getting it wrong gives a 403 identical to sending nothing.

**Challenge:** send it as `Authorization: Bearer …` and confirm you get 403.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 5 — PUT vs PATCH

| Method | Means | A field you leave out |
|---|---|---|
| `PUT` | replace the whole thing | is wiped |
| `PATCH` | change only what I send | is left alone |

**Expected:** `200`, `Patched`, `Brown`, `222` — the last two prove PATCH left them alone.

Try the same with `put` and only a `firstname`: this API rejects it, because a replace needs
the complete object.

Caution for real work: plenty of teams accept partial data on `PUT` anyway. Read the docs,
then test what actually happens — as you just did.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 6 — delete, and prove it

**Objective:** remove the booking, then verify instead of trusting.

**Expected:** `delete -> 201 Created`, `get after delete -> 404`

**`201` for a delete is odd** — the usual convention is `204 No Content`. It doesn't matter:
your job is to test what the API *does*. Assert `204` because a course said so and your test
fails against a working API.

The second call is what makes this a real test. A delete that reports success and deletes
nothing is a genuine bug, and only the follow-up `404` catches it.

| Code | Means | Seen when |
|---|---|---|
| `200` | worked, here's data | most successes |
| `201` | worked, something new exists | creates — and this API's deletes |
| `204` | worked, nothing to return | most deletes, elsewhere |
| `400` | your data was malformed | a missing required field |
| `403` | not allowed | missing or wrong token |
| `404` | no such thing | deleted or invented id |

200s = success. 400s = your fault. 500s = the server's fault.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Now the real thing: a spec file

Cells remember things between runs. A test can't — it must set itself up.

Getting the token is a **prerequisite**, not the thing under test, so it goes in `beforeAll`
and lands in a `let` at the top of the file. Exactly the Day 1.1 situation.

The cell below writes a real spec to disk and runs it with genuine `npx playwright test`.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week8/generated/day1-booking-flow.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `6 passed`, ~5 seconds.

Two things changed by moving into the runner:

- **`expect()` replaced `console.log()`.** You judged the output; now the test judges it.
  That's the whole difference between exploring and testing.
- **`test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" })`.** Each step uses the previous step's
  booking, and Playwright runs tests in parallel by default. Being explicit about the
  dependency is honest; hoping the order works out is how flaky suites start.

Needing serial mode is a smell, though. A test that makes its own data can run alone, in any
order. Day 1.3 shows that version.

## Best practices

- **Make your own data**, and use the id you got back.
- **Fetch tokens at runtime.** Never paste one into a file.
- **Assert more than the status code.** `200` only means the server answered.
- **Verify deletes.** A delete isn't proven by its own status code.
- **Base URL in one place**, so the suite can point at staging.
- **Print the body when confused** — faster than reasoning about it.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `No tests found` | wrong path or filename | copy the path, don't type it |
| `Cannot read properties of undefined` | an earlier dot is wrong | print the whole body |
| `403` / "bad credential" | missing token, or right token in the wrong header | check `Cookie` vs `Authorization` |
| `Promise { <pending> }` | missing `await` | two per call |
| passes alone, fails in the suite | tests sharing data | make each test create its own |
| `Cannot assign to 'token'` | `const token` inside the hook | drop the `const` |

**Next:** [Day 1.3](/learn/w8/d1/p3) — the same code, organised so the 60th test isn't a
copy-paste of the 6th.

parts.title: The same calls, the way a project writes them

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 1.3 — The same calls, the way a project writes them

Every method here is one you ran in [Day 1.2](/learn/w8/d1/p2). **No new API.** The only new
thing is the structure around it — much easier to absorb when the code is already familiar.

## Measure before you refactor

Don't take my word that yesterday's file needs work. Count.

**The base URL scores 1.** You already did that one right — it's a `const` at the top, so
moving to staging is a single edit. Good instinct; keep it.

The other two are the friction:

- The **endpoint path** is rebuilt in every test. Each one has to get the URL right.
- The **auth header** is spelled out once per authenticated call. The day this API moves to
  bearer tokens, that's an edit in every one of them — and missing one gives you a 403 you'll
  spend an afternoon on.

There's a subtler cost too: *every test knows the token travels in a cookie.* That's a fact
about how the API works, and it has leaked into code that only wants to **use** the API.

The fix is the page-object idea applied to an API: **put the knowledge of how the API works
in one place; let tests describe what should be true.**

| Day 1.2 | Here | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `api.put(`${BASE}/booking/${id}`, …)` | `api.update(id, changes)` | the URL is built in one place |
| `` Cookie: `token=${token}` `` in each call | `this.authHeaders()` | one line to change |
| `beforeAll` in every spec file | an `api` fixture | requested by name, not copy-pasted |
| `let token` visible file-wide | `private token` | no test can corrupt it |
| `expect()` mixed into the flow | `expect()` only in tests | client asks, test judges |

## The client

Same six calls, wearing a coat.

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| `readonly` on `request`, `base` | set once; swapping them mid-test becomes a compile error |
| `private token` | exactly one place can set it — `signIn()` |
| `authHeaders()` is a method | the token doesn't exist when the object is built |
| `create` / `read` / `update` / `remove` | intent, not plumbing (`postToBookingEndpoint`) |
| `Partial<Booking>` | PATCH takes *some* fields; stops you passing a full object by accident |
| `?? ""` | a failed login has no token; empty string fails fast instead of sending `undefined` |

Notice `create` isn't `async`. It returns the promise `request.post` gave it — nothing to
wait for in between, so nothing to await. The caller awaits. Adding `async` would work but
say something untrue.

## The rule: no assertions in the client

There isn't one `expect()` in `BookingApi`. Same rule as "no assertions in a page object".

Tempting to assert `200` inside `create()` and save every test a line. But then `create()`
only serves tests that expect success. The rejected-create test needs a second method; the
duplicate-booking test a third. You end up with `createExpectingSuccess`,
`createExpectingFailure`, `createExpectingConflict` — three methods making one call.

**The client knows how to ask. The test decides what the answer should be.**

Worth being able to explain, not just recite — it's a common interview question.
## Running it for real

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week8/generated/day1-api-client.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `2 passed`, ~3 seconds.

Read what the test says now:

```ts
const created = await api.create(sample);
expect(created.status()).toBe(200);
const patched = await api.update(id, { firstname: "Grace" });
```

No URLs, no headers, no token — a description of behaviour. If this API moved to bearer
tokens tomorrow, the test wouldn't change at all. Only `authHeaders()` would.

These tests also **don't need `mode: "serial"`**. Each makes its own booking, so they're
independent and run in parallel. The structure didn't just tidy the code — it removed a
real constraint.

## What a reviewer checks

- No `expect()` in the client — the most common first-review comment
- No hardcoded ids; every id read back from a create
- No token in the source
- Base URL in one place, ideally from config or an env var
- Method names describing intent
- **Every test able to run alone** — otherwise it's the one that fails in CI at 3am

**Next:** [Day 1.4](/learn/w8/d1/p4) — your turn, no worked examples.

# Week 8, Day 1.4 — Practice

Three problems, getting harder. No answer key — each one tells you how to check yourself.

Target: **Restful Booker** — `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com`
([docs](https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html)). Credentials `admin` /
`password123`.

Work in the cells below, or write a spec into `week8/generated/`. Problem 3 expects a spec.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? The gap is in [Day 1.1](/learn/w8/d1/p1) or
> [Day 1.2](/learn/w8/d1/p2), not in your ability.

## When you're done

**If this API switched to a bearer token tomorrow, how many lines would you change?**

One means you understood Day 1.3. More means look at where the header gets built — Day 1.2's
version needed four.

**Could two people run your Problem 3 test at the same time?** That's the difference between
a test that works and a test that works in CI.

**Next:** Day 2 — what to do when the API under test is down, checking a response's *shape*
rather than its values, and chaining calls where one booking feeds the next.

problems.statement:
**Build.** A cell that logs in and proves it worked.

1. POST to `/auth` with the demo credentials
2. Check the status is `200`
3. Check a token came back — not *what* it is, just that it's there and not empty
4. Print it

**Check yourself.** You see `200` and a string of letters and numbers. Run it twice: the
token should differ each time.

> **Hint** — in a lesson you have no `expect()`. An `if` and a `console.log` do the job.

**Build.** A booking's whole life, checked at every step.

A hotel wants proof that a booking made via the API can be found again, corrected, and
cancelled — and that cancelling really removes it.

1. Create a booking with **your own** name and dates
2. Read it back by id; confirm the name you sent is the name stored
3. PATCH only the `totalprice`; confirm the guest's name was **not** affected
4. Delete it
5. Prove it's gone

**Check yourself.** Step 5 returns `404`. If it returns `200`, your delete didn't do what
you thought.

> **Hint** — step 2 is where the shape changes between create and read.

**Build.** Your own client and fixture — not a copy of Day 1.3's.

Restful Booker has an endpoint Day 1.3 never touched: `GET /booking` returns every booking
id, and accepts filters like `?firstname=Jim`.

1. A `BookingApi` class with `signIn()`, `create()`, `read()`, `remove()` and a new
   `search(filters)` for the filtered list
2. A fixture so a test can write `async ({ api }) => {}` and get a signed-in client
3. A test that: creates a booking with a distinctive first name, searches for that name,
   confirms the new id is in the results, deletes it, confirms the id is gone

**Where.** A spec in `week8/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `expect()` inside the class**
- **No hardcoded ids** — every id read back from a create
- The test must pass **run on its own**, in any order

**Check yourself.** It passes, then passes twice more in a row. A test that only passes the
first time is leaning on data it left behind.

> **Hint** — pick a genuinely distinctive first name. This is a public API and other people
> are using it; `Jim` will match hundreds of bookings that aren't yours.
